problem: Sim-to-real transfer for navigation is limited: synthetic datasets (HSSD) lack realism, while real scans (HM3D, Matterport) need expensive equipment and cannot cover a specific deployment environment. Pre-trained ImageNav policies generalize poorly to out-of-distribution scenes such as classrooms and lounges.
motivation: Personalizing a policy to its deployment site could close the sim-to-real gap, but this needs a cheap, fast way to reconstruct the site as a simulator-ready mesh. Gaussian Splatting from casual phone captures could provide this, but its use for training and deploying end-to-end indoor navigation policies was unexplored.
key_idea: Capture the deployment scene with an iPhone, reconstruct a mesh with depth/normal-regularized Gaussian Splatting (DN-Splatter) or Polycam, load it into Habitat-Sim, and fine-tune a pre-trained ImageNav policy on it before real-robot deployment.
insight: Short fine-tuning (20M steps) on the reconstructed target scene closes most of the gap for out-of-distribution scenes. Real-world SR on the lounge rose from 50% to 70% for HM3D and from 10% to 50%/40% for HSSD. Zero-shot SR falls with scene scale and rises with the GS validation PSNR. More pre-training on HM3D/HSSD plateaus or degrades zero-shot performance on the new scenes after roughly 300-400M steps. Overfitting from scratch reaches near-perfect sim SR but transfers unevenly (50% Polycam vs 10% DN mesh), which suggests visual fidelity matters and pre-training helps.
method: Scene capture: iPhone 13 Pro Max with the Polycam app (RGB-D, 20-30 min per scene, hand-held); Nerfstudio samples 1000 low-blur aligned RGB-depth frames with poses.

Mesh reconstruction: DN-Splatter trains GS for 30k iterations with sensor depth (λd=0.2), depth smoothness, and normal losses from Metric3D-V2; Poisson reconstruction gives the mesh. Polycam's own mesh serves as a comparison. Encoder choice was validated on the 10 Mushroom scenes.

Simulator integration: convert .ply to .glb in Blender and load into Habitat-Sim. Use only the largest navmesh island, computed with Stretch parameters, and generate 1000 train and 100 val ImageNav episodes per scene.

Policy: VC-1-Base visual encoder with a compression layer, goal/observation encoders sharing weights, and a 2-layer LSTM. Actions are MOVE_FORWARD, TURN_LEFT, TURN_RIGHT, and STOP. Trained with DD-PPO with an ImageNav reward, following Silwal et al.

Training strategies: zero-shot from HM3D (600M steps) or HSSD (1200M steps) pre-training; fine-tuning for 20M steps with low learning rates (2.5e-6 LSTM, 6e-7 encoder); overfitting from scratch on a single scene for ~100M steps.
Real deployment: a Stretch robot without GPU queries a remote Flask policy server via ROS (home-robot); 10 start/goal pairs, 100-step cap, success within 1 m.
Analysis: SRCC sim-vs-real correlation, PSNR/scene-scale correlations, and pre-training-length curves.

setting.backbone: VC-1-Base visual encoder + 2-layer LSTM policy (fine-tuned with DD-PPO); pre-trained on HM3D or HSSD
setting.training_data: Pre-training on HM3D (800 train scenes, 10k episodes/scene) or HSSD (134 train scenes); fine-tuning on 1000 episodes per iPhone-captured scene (4 university scenes plus Mushroom scenes) for 20M steps; overfitting baselines trained from scratch for ~100M steps
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB (640x480, 42° HFOV, resized to 160x120) plus a goal image
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: MOVE_FORWARD, TURN_LEFT, TURN_RIGHT, STOP
setting.privileged: none at test time (goal image only); the target scene is reconstructed beforehand for fine-tuning

results: Fine-tuning for 20M steps on reconstructed scenes raises real-world lounge SR from 50% to 70% (HM3D policy) and from 10% to 50%/40% (HSSD policy). Sim fine-tuned SR is around 90%+ for HM3D and 80%+ for HSSD, and sim-vs-real correlation is reported as 0.87-0.97. Per-scene pre-trained policies from HM3D beat those from HSSD zero-shot.
limitations: Real-world evaluation is small: 10 episodes in a single lounge scene, so the numbers are statistically weak.
GS-derived DN meshes are darker and have holes, which gives lower visual fidelity than Polycam meshes. Scenes are small (1-3 rooms), not apartment-scale.
Fine-tuning is per-scene and needs a new capture and reconstruction (1-2 hours) for each deployment site.
